To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) teachers' implicit notions about children's intelligence are composed of two factors, namely, academic skills and interpersonal competencies; (2) these two factors are affected in a different manner by the intelligence of the child; (3) teachers who are high in dogmatism have more extreme notions of the intellectual abilities of a hypothetical child than do teachers who are low in dogmatism; (4) the effects of the dogmatism and intelligence variables are independent; (5) the
teachers' implicit “theories of intelligence” are not fixed and immutable but rather depend on the context in which they are used.
Teachers, like everyone, have implicit “theory” of intelligence; and that the theory is different for different teachers and depends on the situation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a theory of intelligence that is more comprehensive and more useful for educational purposes than the one currently in use.
the question of how people, in particular teachers, think about intelligence.
the development and testing of an implicit “theory” model of intelligence.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
teachers have implicit “theoriest” of intelligence which are influenced by their dogmatism and their level of experience.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
teachers' implicit “theories of intelligence” are a function of the interaction of dogmatism and years of experience.
teachers, as well as other people, have implicit “theorizing” of children's intelligence that are influenced by their own dogmatism and the context in which they find themselves.
teachers' implicit notions about children's intelligence are not a simple reflection of their dogmatism and/or experience.
The main takeaway from our work is that
teachers have implicit “theorie” of children's intelligence that can be measured by the Implicit Theories of Children's Intelligence Scale.
the implicit theories of intelligence are not stable, and that teachers' implicit theories of children's intelligence change depending on the situation.
teachers' implicit notions are not static, but vary with the context within which they are applied.
